• Other names: Nimble Spray crab, Short crab, Urchin Crab
  • Minimum tank size: 60 litres
  • Breeding: Very Difficult
  • Size: 7–12 cm across the leg span; carapace length up to 3.8 cm
  • Water type: SG 1.023–1.025
  • KH: 8–12
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: Omnivore
  • Temperament: Semi-aggressive
  • Life span: up to 5 years
  • Colours: Brown, Orange, Yellow, Blue

Warning: NEVER release Percnon gibbesi into the wild due to its potential to become invasive. For example, this crab has been proposed to be included in the 100 worst invasive marine species at the European level.

The native range of the Sally Lightfoot Crab is extensive. It is found on the Pacific coasts of Mexico, Central and South America, the Atlantic coast of South America, the Western Atlantic from Florida to Brazil, and the Eastern Atlantic from Madeira, the Azores and the Cape Verde Islands to the coast of Africa, from Morocco to Ghana, and offshore islands of the Gulf of Guinea.

In about 15 years, it has virtually colonized the entire Mediterranean Sea, becoming one of the most widespread non-native species found in Mediterranean waters.

Basically, Percnon gibbesi can be found worldwide in tropical-temperate waters.

Sally Lightfoot Crabs are strictly subtidal and occupy shallow hard bottoms, usually on rocky shores at 1–2 m depth, among boulders covered by algae.

In the wild, they tend to show a very patchy distribution and aggregate in groups of more than two individuals.
Use a saltwater tank with a capacity of at least 60 litres that has plenty of rocks and caves for the crab to hide in.

Keeping Sally Lightfoot Crabs is simple. They are very hardy.

In the wild, this species showed a preference for boulder fields with surfaces covered with encrusting algae or algal turf. However, it was never observed on sandy bottoms, bottoms with sparse boulders, or in seagrass meadows. Keep this in mind when choosing the substrate.

They do not need any additional supplements to survive in captivity, but ensure the tank water stays warm, at 22–25°C. Although this species can tolerate a wide range of water temperatures, its survival might be challenging at low winter temperatures of 15°C or less.

As these animals are used to the turbulent waters of the ocean shore, a tank with a medium to strong current is ideal.

An added bonus is that they act as tank janitors, cleaning the substrate and rocks in the aquarium.

Consistent water parameters are the cornerstone of any successful aquarium. Make sure they are kept within a suitable range at all times and do not fluctuate.

Before putting them in the tank, do not forget to acclimate them.

Molting

Molting is a key stage in the life cycle. More molts indicate a healthy and rapidly growing animal. Seeing the molted shells is a great way to gauge the health of the crab.

Molting is another reason it is critical to maintain a sufficient number of rocks and other hiding spots. Sally Lightfoot Crabs are extremely vulnerable in this soft-shell phase and need a place to hide safely while their shells harden.

Like all invertebrates, Sally Lightfoot Crabs need calcium to mineralize (harden) the shell. Calcium is vital for good shell growth.
Temperature 22–25°C; SG 1.023–1.025; pH 8.0–8.4; KH 8–12; GH 8–12 °d; nitrate less than 20 ppm.

Sally Lightfoot Crabs are not picky eaters and make great "reef janitors" in a well-established aquarium. They eat scraps of leftover food as well as many different varieties of algae and detritus.

They feed primarily on algae (including a wide variety of algal meals), but also on animal food (such as copepods, worms, snails, crustaceans and jellyfish), and are considered opportunistic feeders.

They can eat filamentous algae, calcareous algae, foliose algae, Stypocaulon scoparium, Hypnea musciformis, Liagora viscida, Gelidium crinale, Sphacelaria sp., Caulerpa racemosa, Jania rubens, Padina pavonica, Dictyopteris polypodioides, etc.

Field observations suggest that plant material constitutes the bulk of the diet; however, in some cases animal matter made up 43.2% of the stomach contents. This feeding flexibility is probably a key factor that has facilitated their worldwide spread.

If there are not enough leftovers or algae in the tank to sustain your crabs, consider supplementing the diet with store-bought food such as dried seaweed or other meaty treats.

Sally Lightfoot Crabs are relatively easy to care for, but they have a semi-aggressive temperament, which may put off some potential owners.

Aggression is latent until they grow to adult size. At that point they may become aggressive and will likely attack small prey in the tank, such as invertebrates and small fish.

They can be very difficult to catch as they are very quick on their feet, have an incredibly fast reaction time and can jump. These adaptations are their main defence in predator-heavy natural habitats and stay with them in captivity.

Once full-grown, they have virtually no natural predators in their native habitat because of their speed, hard shell and other defensive adaptations. They can even shed a leg or spray water at attackers in moments of extreme distress. There is no need to panic if you observe these behaviours.

A Sally Lightfoot Crab generally spends most of its time scavenging around the tank and keeping out of sight behind and between rocks and any structures in the aquarium. They become most active towards dusk.

Tankmates

They get along especially well with other members of their own species.

They will, however, compete with tankmates for food, which can also affect their behaviour. To mitigate this, make sure the crab is well fed at all times.

It is risky to house Sally Lightfoot Crabs with small and peaceful fish, shrimp and snails, as they will likely begin to prey on them eventually.

However, they will not bother most animals that are their size or larger. For example, the marbled rock crab (Proterorhinus marmoratus) completely dominates over Sally Lightfoot Crabs. Even a large or medium-sized Sally Lightfoot Crab was never observed to injure or kill smaller marbled rock crabs.

Sally Lightfoot Crabs are considered reef-safe and will not attack living corals. However, they may attack and eat invertebrates and small fish as they age and become larger and more aggressive.

Sexing can be somewhat tricky for an inexperienced owner, made harder by the active nature and speed of these animals. You need to examine the underside of the crab to tell male from female.

Males generally have a thinner abdominal width than females, which have a much wider abdomen.

According to biologists, male chela (claw) length shows a much larger positive allometry (disproportionally larger) than that of females, which show low positive allometry.

Sexual dimorphism seems to appear at an early stage of the life cycle. At a carapace length as small as 12–13 mm, male chela length shows an upward inflection relative to that of the female. The sexual dimorphism of the chelae may be a consequence of their use by the male in combat, display and courtship.

Due to many different factors, breeding presents various difficulties and it is really hard to replicate all the conditions at home. So far there have been no reports of successful breeding of Sally Lightfoot Crab in captivity. Even biologists have not achieved it in their experiments.

Analysis of abdomen morphology suggested that females reach sexual maturity at a carapace length of 15.0–16.0 mm. Assessment of size at sexual maturity using abdomen morphology gave identical results for males.

In the wild, they breed during the summer months.

Berried females carry eggs on their abdomen until they are ready to hatch, at which point they release the eggs into the ocean. Brood size of mature ovigerous females ranges between 250 and 32,000 eggs per brood. There is a significant correlation between the number of eggs per brood and the size of the female.

Like most marine organisms, they have a larval phase (locomotion at this stage is usually limited to vertical movements) followed by a megalopa phase that can actively swim and reach the habitat where settlement occurs. If the larvae survive enough molts, they undergo metamorphosis and enter the juvenile stage.

There is no information on how long it takes larvae to metamorphose into baby crabs. Biologists examined the substrate preference and settlement behaviour of megalopae using three natural substrates in an experimental mesocosm: gravel, cobbles and flat stones. A strong preference was shown for hard and stable substrates, i.e. cobbles and flat stones with interstices in which to hide, which are also the most suitable as they provide shelter and food.

They prefer to settle on a physically stable substrate that offers narrow interstices for hiding rather than on mobile substrates like gravel or sand.

The Sally Lightfoot Crab is on the smaller end and can reach a maximum size of 7–12 cm across the leg span. Carapace length usually ranges from 25 to 37 mm.

Coloration of adults varies; a reddish-brown colour with orange and yellow details is typical, but they can vary from blue to red to spotted and even pink. These bright colours are an important part of sexual selection.

Young crabs are almost always brown or black. They are vulnerable at this stage and these neutral colours let them blend in with their surroundings on rocky shorelines.

The body is disk-like, slightly oval and flattened, with two identically sized, thick claws. All have five pairs of legs with visible rings, and two front antennae on top of the head, which are almost always in motion.

Young crabs have relatively soft shells, so take care when handling; the shell hardens significantly as the animal grows older.
